text_mt:
Having seen Skanda, whose brilliance was equal to blazing fire, / the lord of the gods praised him, O tiger among kings, disciplined and well-composed.
Śakra said: / I bow to the god of gods, Kumāra, the excellent, unfallen one, / Kārtikeya, difficult to appease, born of the fire's brilliance.
[I bow to him] born of Umā and Śaṅkara, fierce, borne in the womb by Gaṅgā, / holding a spear in his hand, large-eyed, six-faced, and of blazing splendour,
compassionate to his devotees, subdued, devoted to brahmins, grantor of boons, the lord, / wearing side-locks of hair, tranquil, adorned with crest-feathers,
wearing red garments, mighty-armed, riding upon an excellent peacock, / fond of bells, leader of the troops, of great strength and valor,
the god who is the commander of the army of the gods, desiring the welfare of all the worlds. / And those who, on the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight, on a Tuesday,
worship you during [the asterism of] the Kṛttikās individually according to their means, / nothing will be difficult for them to obtain, O foremost of the gods.

he slew the Dānava named Mahiṣa, the thorn in the side of the gods; / and he slew tens of thousands of others equal in prowess to Mahiṣa.
When the heroic Skanda, crusher of enemy armies, was unable / to slay the Dānavas on account of their vast numbers, then the three-eyed god,
whose supreme weapon is the trident, slew [them] there with his mind, / and then slew other Dānavas by hundreds and by thousands.
Having struck down the hosts of the gods' enemies in battle, the Lord with three eyes, compassionate to devotees, / and having then caused the three worlds to rejoice, the great-souled one went to Mount Kailāsa.
1.234 / Nāḍāyana said: / Hear another display of power of that very god of gods: / formerly, when no share in the sacrifice was designated for the three-eyed one
by the gods wishing to sacrifice, O king, then by the enraged Śambhu, / having gone to the sacrificial enclosure, the gods were violently terrified.
Having devoured the sacrificial cake, he knocked out the teeth of Pūṣan; / the slayer of enemy heroes broke the left eye of Bhaga.

text_mt:
Seeing Mahādeva enraged, the Sacrifice, taking the form of a deer, / then fled at once to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Hara of great splendour, holding bow and arrows, pursued it. / When Hara arrived, holding bow and arrows and pursuing the Sacrifice,
Nārāyaṇa threw him into confusion by seizing his throat. / While Mahādeva was in distress, the Sacrifice then took refuge in heaven.
Hara, too, regaining consciousness, quickly pursued it in heaven. / When Dharma, by his splendour, could not pierce the deer,
then Brahmā, auspicious and four-faced, enlightened him. / Then he granted complete favour once again to Bhaga,
and granting safety to the Sacrifice, he playfully pursued it again. / And the star-deer in the sky, ever following Mahādeva,
is seen at night as an ornament of the sky, O fortunate one.
When enraged, Rudra cast down the gods, and when pleased, he restored them once again; / therefore, when pleased he leads to welfare in the world, and when enraged he is declared the destroyer of the worlds.

1.235 / Nāḍāyana said: / Hear another display of power of that very god of gods: / when the sacrifice of the wise Dakṣa was destroyed by him,
when Dakṣa was sacrificing long ago at Gaṅgādvāra, O lord, / because Śarva was not invited, the Goddess became enraged.
And on account of the Goddess’s fury, the wielder of the trident was then enraged, / and created an attendant known as Vīrabhadra, born of his anger.
Then Pārvatī created Bhadrakālī from her own body. / Accompanied by the attendants, O king, the renowned Vīrabhadra,
together with Bhadrakālī, went and destroyed Dakṣa's sacrifice. / And Śiva, accompanied by Pārvatī,
beholding the sacrifice being destroyed, remained there as Bhadrakarṇeśvara, O lord of kings. / But while the sacrifice was being destroyed, Dakṣa spoke these words

Having reached the sacrificial ground of the Prajāpati, by that very virtue / one will be freed from all sin and will go to heaven.
Water found in the ground is more meritorious than drawn [water], spring water is more meritorious than that; / lake water is declared even more meritorious than that; / waterfall water is more meritorious than lake water, and river water even more than waterfall water.

at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. / At Gaṅgādvāra, at Kuśāvarta, at Bilvaka, at Nīlaparvata,

text_mt: 1.236 / Nāḍāyana said: / Hear another manifestation of the power of that god who bears the trident, / how Śveta was liberated by him when he had fallen into the power of Death.
title: Kāladāraṇaḥ

sanskrit_iast:

sanskrit_iast:
tasya pūjāprasaktasya kadācitpṛthivīpate ..

आजगाम तमुद्देशं कालः परमदारुणः .. 3 ..

sanskrit_iast:
raktavṛttatrinayanaḥ sarpavṛścikaromavān ..
daṃṣṭrākarālo vikaṭaḥ cūrṇitāñjanasaprabhaḥ .. 4 ..

text_mt: while I complete my worship of the enemy of Manmatha!" / Then Time laughed and spoke to him, O ruler of the earth:

text_mt:
Nāḍāyana said: / Invisible, supreme, pure, proclaimed of old and destroying sin, / removing sorrow is the armour I speak to you of, by which protection was made by Maheśvara.
1.237 / Maheśvara said: / Having bowed to the unaging, the sovereign, unborn, eternal, free from disease, / the god who is the Lord of All, Viṣṇu, all-pervading and imperishable,
having bowed to Janārdana, I bind the protective amulet, / unfailing, unobstructed, warding off all wicked things.
May Viṣṇu protect in front of me; may Kṛṣṇa guard behind. / May Hari guard my head, and Janārdana my heart.
May Hṛṣīkeśa protect my mind; may Keśava guard my tongue. / May Vāsudeva protect my eyes, and Saṃkarṣaṇa my ears.
May Pradyumna protect my nose, and Aniruddha my mouth. / May he who wears a forest garland protect my throat; may the Śrīvatsa-chested protect in front; / and may the discus, the tearer of Daityas, protect my left side;

text_mt:
and the divine club, warding off all Asuras, my right [side]. / May the wielder of the pestle protect my belly, and the wielder of the plough my back.
May the wielder of the bow Śārṅga guard my thighs; may the wielder of the shield guard my shanks. / May the wielder of the conch guard my hands, and both my feet, my two limbs. / For the accomplishment of all aims and tasks, may he whose banner is Garuḍa protect me.
May the Boar protect in water, and the Dwarf in rough places. / In the forest, indeed, Narasiṃha; and may Keśava protect on every side.
May the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha bestow gold upon me; / and may Kapila, the teacher of Sāṃkhya, effect equilibrium of my bodily humours.
And may the unborn dweller in Śvetadvīpa lead [me] to Śvetadvīpa. / May the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha destroy all enemies.
May Viṣṇu ever pull away sin from my body. / May the Swan, the Fish, and the Tortoise protect me in every direction.
May the god Trivikrama sever all my fetters; / may the god Nara-Nārāyaṇa preserve my intellect.

text_mt:
May Śeṣa, possessing boundless pure knowledge, destroy [my] ignorance. / May the Submarine Fire destroy the stain that has been done by me.
May the horse-headed Lord grant supreme knowledge to me; / may Dattātreya protect [me] together with sons, livestock, and kin.
May Rāma with his axe destroy all diseases of mine; / may the son of Daśaratha, slayer of Rakṣasas, mighty-armed, ever protect me.
May Rāma, delight of the Yādavas, strike down my foes with his plough; / he who slew Pralamba, Keśin, Cāṇūra, Pūtanā, and Kaṃsa,
Kṛṣṇa who was in the state of a child, may he grant my desires. / Deep darkness, dreadful gloom, a dark and reddish-brown person,
I see, tormented by fear, like Death with a noose in his hand. / Thereupon I have gone for refuge to the lotus-eyed, unfalling one,
the Lord of Yogins abiding in transcendent form, spotless as the auspicious cool-rayed [moon]. / Blessed am I, ever victorious, whose [protector] is the Blessed Hari.
Remembering the god Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all calamities, / having bound on the Vaiṣṇava armour, I wander upon the surface of the earth.

text_mt: Svāhā to time! / Svāhā to the person of time! / Svāhā to the fierce one! / Svāhā to the fierce person! / Svāhā to the All! / Svāhā to the All of All! / Oṃ, reverence to the Lord of the world, whose abode is the three worlds: itiṭi piriṭi svāhā! / Oṃ, by the highest […] for me, O wind, for me; whatever beings walk in evil—among them daityas, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, apasmāras, lunacy, and the fevers: quotidian, tertian, quartan, four-day, hourly, day-fever, night-fever, continuous fever, twilight fever, and the destruction of all fevers and the rest; spiders, insects, thorns, kaṭapūtanās, serpents, stationary poisons, virulent poisons, and the rest—may this body of mine be invincible! Oṃ, with a good syllable, he acts: fierce, terrible-fanged one, protect from the east! / Oṃ haiṃ haiṃ haiṃ haiṃ, fierce brilliance equal to the radiance of a thousand suns, protect, protect from the west! / Oṃ, blazing fire in burning flames, black with time, great yellow-haired ascetic with matted locks, protect from the north! / Oṃ cilicili milimili cekaḍi gauri gāndhāri poison-destroyer, may poison bewilder me, svāhā! / Protect me, [insert name], from the south, from the dangers and afflictions of all beings, svāhā! / Victory triumphs, may the grant of victory arise! The destroyer of enemy cities does not strike; dispelling fear from the heart, bestowing fear, may this noble Acyuta grant fearlessness to fear! / Into whose belly all rays enter, / having beginning and end, the ancient seers, subtle, immense, the rulers— / may Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva destroy all fevers for me!

1.238 / Vajra said: / Having heard the burning of Kālāṅga spoken by the brahmin, / what did Śailūṣa, driven by death, then ask, O holy one?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Having heard the burning of Kālāṅga spoken by the brahmin, / he then asked him again about the deeds of Rāvaṇa alone.
Śailūṣa said: / What remains of the deeds of the ten-necked rākṣasa, / that I wish to hear; I have great doubt about it.
Nāḍāyana said: / Then Rāvaṇa walked all around his city once more. / He then saw there an entirely golden mansion,
surrounded by nets of pearls, with arches of coral, / and with an altar made entirely of emerald and ruby,
with beautiful pillars of lapis lazuli, blazing with the lustre of rubies, / covered with the radiance of sapphires, adorned with hundreds of turrets,
crowded with great halls, adorned with a great garden, / having stairs easy to ascend, filled with hundreds of oblong ponds,

If you would fight with him, O hero, enter this excellent house; / [yet] you should not fight with him: he is great-souled and possesses great strength.

resembling refined gold, shining brightly like blazing fire, / the god bearing a universal form, bestowing boons, assuming forms at will.

The Viśvedevas were on his waist; the Maruts at the top of his bladder; / the goddess Earth was at his feet, and Piśācas rested on his nails.
In his middle were the eight Vasus; the oceans rested in his belly; / and in his sides were all the directions; the wind was in all his joints.

and gifts of gold were between the hairs of his liver; / and in the parts of his bones were mountains, and likewise rivers in his blood vessels.

“Who are you who lie upon the couch, resembling the fire at the end of the age?” / Addressed thus by him, he then replied to the night-roamer:
“What [concern] have you with me, O ten-necked one? You are to be slain by me before long; / and in this very manner your death will occur, O ten-faced one.
She whom you wish to seize out of delusion, you shall abduct her again; / having attained human form, I will slay you, O Rāvaṇa.
For the sake of this large-eyed lady [I spare you]; depart now, O rākṣasa.” / Hearing these words from the god, Rāvaṇa said:
“There is none more fortunate in the world, in all the three worlds, than me, / whose death will come from your hand, O Lord of the Universe!
Fame-bringing and praiseworthy is my death at your hands.” / Then, Rāvaṇa of terrifying valour looked upon his body.

sanskrit_iast:

ramayanti priyānyatra vanamālākṛtasrajaḥ ..5..

कर्पूरचन्दनार्द्रांग्यो मृणालवलयाः प्रियाः ..
रमयन्ति प्रियान्यत्र वनमालाकृतस्रजः ..5..

sanskrit_iast:

ramaṇīyapradoṣāśca sutarāṃ yatra rātrayaḥ .. 6 ..

रमणीयप्रदोषाश्च सुतरां यत्र रात्रयः .. 6 ..
text_mt: where the rays of the moon, heightening desire in lovers, were sought after, / and where the evenings were delightful, and nights especially so;

sanskrit_iast:
rātryante śītalānvātānkusumāśayagandhinaḥ ..
samāghrāyābhijāyante kāminastu riraṃsavaḥ .. 7 ..
meaning:
रात्र्यन्ते शीतलान्वातान्कुसुमाशयगन्धिनः ..
समाघ्रायाभिजायन्ते कामिनस्तु रिरंसवः .. 7 ..
text_mt: where, at the end of the night, breathing in the cool winds / fragrant with the scent of flowers, lovers became eager for amorous play;

sanskrit_iast:
rātrayaḥ śīghragāminyo divasā mandagāminaḥ ..
mithunopagamādbhānoḥ saṃprataptā bhṛśaṃ karāḥ .. 8 ..
meaning:
रात्रयः शीघ्रगामिन्यो दिवसा मन्दगामिनः ..
मिथुनोपगमाद्भानोः संप्रतप्ता भृशं कराः .. 8 ..
text_mt: where nights passed swiftly and days moved slowly, / and the rays of the sun became intensely hot because of its entry into Gemini;

sanskrit_iast:
vilīnahimatoyaugha phenapuñjasamākulāḥ ..
atyarthaśītāḥ saritastathā haimena parvatāḥ .. 9 ..

विलीनहिमतोयौघ फेनपुञ्जसमाकुलाः ..
अत्यर्थशीताः सरितस्तथा हैमेन पर्वताः .. 9 ..

vardhayanti tathā kāmaṃ kāminīnāṃ tu kāmukāḥ .. 1.241.10 ..

text_mt: and with sandalwood perfumed by abundant resin, / lovers heightened the passion of passionate women;

sanskrit_iast:
ratyantarasamutpannamāyāsaśramajaṃ jalam ..
karpūrarajasā yatra nāśayanti sma kāminaḥ .. 11 ..
meaning:
रत्यन्तरसमुत्पन्नमायासश्रमजं जलम् ..
कर्पूररजसा यत्र नाशयन्ति स्म कामिनः .. 11 ..
text_mt: where lovers wiped away the sweat born of fatigue and exertion / produced at the end of intercourse with camphor powder;

sanskrit_iast:
yasminnidāghe saphalāmravṛkṣe vibhūṣaṇāḍhyo nṛpa vatsarasya ..
didṛkṣavastaṃ raghuvṛnda mukhyaṃ tadā prayātā punayastvayodhyām .. 12 ..
1.242
nāḍāyana uvāca ..
tataḥ sabhāgataṃ rāmaṃ dvāḥstho vacanamabravīt ..
dvāri tiṣṭhanti munayo yamunātīravāsinaḥ ..1..
bhārgavaṃ tu puraskṛtya cyavanaṃ dīptatejasam ..
mahānubhāvā varadāstapasā dagdhakilbiṣāḥ .. 2 ..
dvāḥsthāttu vacanaṃ śrutvā tadā rāmaḥ purodhasā ..
sahitastvarayā draṣṭuṃ tāpasām̐stānvinirgataḥ .. 3 ..
so'bhigamya mahātejā ṛṣisaṅghāṃstapasvinaḥ ..
abhivādya praṇamyaitānpuraskṛtya tadā gṛham .. 4 ..
prāveśayattatasteṣāṃ pādyārghyācamanādikam ..
āsanaṃ madhuparkaṃ ca tathā rājyaṃ nyavedayat .. 5 ..
pratigṛhya tu te sarve rājyaṃ tasmai punardaduḥ ..
tadvacca tīrthatoyāni phalāni vividhāni ca .. 6 ..
meaning:
यस्मिन्निदाघे सफलाम्रवृक्षे विभूषणाढ्यो नृप वत्सरस्य ..
दिदृक्षवस्तं रघुवृन्द मुख्यं तदा प्रयाता पुनयस्त्वयोध्याम् .. 12 ..

नाडायन उवाच ..
ततः सभागतं रामं द्वाःस्थो वचनमब्रवीत् ..
द्वारि तिष्ठन्ति मुनयो यमुनातीरवासिनः ..1..

महानुभावा वरदास्तपसा दग्धकिल्बिषाः .. 2 ..
द्वाःस्थात्तु वचनं श्रुत्वा तदा रामः पुरोधसा ..
सहितस्त्वरया द्रष्टुं तापसाम्̐स्तान्विनिर्गतः .. 3 ..
सोऽभिगम्य महातेजा ऋषिसङ्घांस्तपस्विनः ..
अभिवाद्य प्रणम्यैतान्पुरस्कृत्य तदा गृहम् .. 4 ..
प्रावेशयत्ततस्तेषां पाद्यार्घ्याचमनादिकम् ..
आसनं मधुपर्कं च तथा राज्यं न्यवेदयत् .. 5 ..
प्रतिगृह्य तु ते सर्वे राज्यं तस्मै पुनर्ददुः ..
तद्वच्च तीर्थतोयानि फलानि विविधानि च .. 6 ..

in that summer, rich in fruit-bearing mango trees, an ornament of the year, O king, / sages wishing to see that foremost of the line of Raghu then set out for Ayodhyā.
1.242
Nāḍāyana said:
Then the doorkeeper spoke to Rāma, who had arrived at the assembly hall: / “Sages residing on the banks of the Yamunā stand at the gate,
placing foremost the descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana of blazing splendor— / high-souled, bestowers of boons, whose sins are burned away by ascetic austerity.”
Hearing the words from the doorkeeper, Rāma then, accompanied by his family priest, / swiftly went out to see those ascetics.
Approaching the ascetic hosts of sages, that one of great splendour / greeted them, bowed down to them, and then, leading them forward, into his house
he brought them; then water for their feet, guest-water, sipping-water, and the like, / a seat, and honey-mixture, and likewise he offered his kingdom.
Having accepted it, they all gave the kingdom back to him, / and likewise sacred waters and various fruits.

sanskrit_iast:
pratigṛhya ca rāmastānpṛṣṭvā kuśalamavyamam ..
papraccha tānmahābhāgastatastvāgamanakriyām .. 7 ..
rāmasya vacanaṃ śrutvā cyavano vākyamabravīt ..
rākṣaso lavaṇo nāma rājanmadhuvane vasan..8..
lokāṃstāpayate sarvāṃstasya yatnaṃ vadhe kuru ..
daśaprāṇisahasrāṇi cāhārastasya naityikaḥ .. 9 ..
vadhārthaṃ bharataṃ tasya śatrughnaṃ sahalakṣmaṇam ..
samā diśa mahābhāga lokāḥ santu nirāmayāḥ .. 1.242.10 ..
tathā madhuvane sphīte deśaṃ rāma niveśaya ..
nagarīñca yathā puṇyāṃ lokānāṃ hitakāmyayā ..11 ..
tvayā sa bhājyo rakṣyāśca munisaṃghā mahāmate ..
evamuktastadā rāmaścintayāmāsa dharmavit .. 12 ..
meaning:
प्रतिगृह्य च रामस्तान्पृष्ट्वा कुशलमव्यमम् ..
पप्रच्छ तान्महाभागस्ततस्त्वागमनक्रियाम् .. 7 ..
रामस्य वचनं श्रुत्वा च्यवनो वाक्यमब्रवीत् ..
राक्षसो लवणो नाम राजन्मधुवने वसन्..8..
लोकांस्तापयते सर्वांस्तस्य यत्नं वधे कुरु ..
दशप्राणिसहस्राणि चाहारस्तस्य नैत्यिकः .. 9 ..
वधार्थं भरतं तस्य शत्रुघ्नं सहलक्ष्मणम् ..
समा दिश महाभाग लोकाः सन्तु निरामयाः .. 1.242.10 ..
तथा मधुवने स्फीते देशं राम निवेशय ..
नगरीञ्च यथा पुण्यां लोकानां हितकाम्यया ..11 ..
त्वया स भाज्यो रक्ष्याश्च मुनिसंघा महामते ..
एवमुक्तस्तदा रामश्चिन्तयामास धर्मवित् .. 12 ..
text_mt:
Having received [these] and enquired after their unfailing welfare, / the illustrious Rāma then asked them the purpose of their arrival.
Hearing Rāma's words, Cyavana spoke [these] words: / "O king, a rākṣasa named Lavaṇa, dwelling in the Madhu forest,
torments all the worlds; make an effort for his slaying! / Ten thousand living beings are his daily food.
Command Bharata, or Śatrughna together with Lakṣmaṇa, / for his slaying, O illustrious one, so that the worlds may be free from suffering.
Likewise, settle a territory in the flourishing Madhu forest, O Rāma, / and a sacred city, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
He must be destroyed by you, and the hosts of sages must be protected, O wise one!" / Thus addressed then, Rāma, who knew dharma, reflected:

sanskrit_iast:
lakṣmaṇena mahatkarma kṛtaṃ nivasatā vane ..
rājyaṃ pālayatā karma bharatena mahatkṛtam .. 13 ..
meaning:
लक्ष्मणेन महत्कर्म कृतं निवसता वने ..
राज्यं पालयता कर्म भरतेन महत्कृतम् .. 13 ..
text_mt: "A great deed was accomplished by Lakṣmaṇa while dwelling in the forest; / a great deed was accomplished by Bharata while protecting the kingdom.

sanskrit_iast:
śatrughnaṃ prerayāmyadya lavaṇasya vadhepsayā ..
ityevaṃ cintayitvā tu rāmaḥ śatrughnamabravīt .. 14 ..
meaning:
शत्रुघ्नं प्रेरयाम्यद्य लवणस्य वधेप्सया ..
इत्येवं चिन्तयित्वा तु रामः शत्रुघ्नमब्रवीत् .. 14 ..
text_mt: I shall send Śatrughna today with the desire to slay Lavaṇa." / Having thus reflected, Rāma said to Śatrughna:

sanskrit_iast:
munīṃścaitānpuraskatya gaccha śatrughna mā ciram ..
ghātayasva durācāraṃ lavaṇaṃ pāpakāriṇam .. 15 ..
meaning:
मुनींश्चैतान्पुरस्कत्य गच्छ शत्रुघ्न मा चिरम् ..
घातयस्व दुराचारं लवणं पापकारिणम् .. 15 ..
text_mt: "Placing these sages at the head, go, Śatrughna; do not delay! / Cause the wicked, evil-doing Lavaṇa to be slain!

sanskrit_iast:
ghātayitvā ca lavaṇaṃ janāṃstatra niveśaya ..
nagarī ca tathā tatra tvayā kāryā manoramā .. 16 ..
meaning:
घातयित्वा च लवणं जनांस्तत्र निवेशय ..
नगरी च तथा तत्र त्वया कार्या मनोरमा .. 16 ..
text_mt: And having caused Lavaṇa to be slain, settle people there, / and likewise a charming city must be built by you there.

sanskrit_iast:
tasyāṃ vasa mahābhāga pālayam̐stvaṃ vasundharām ..
tatrāhamabhiṣekṣyāmi rājye tvāmṛṣibhiḥ saha .. 17 ..
meaning:
तस्यां वस महाभाग पालयम्̐स्त्वं वसुन्धराम् ..
तत्राहमभिषेक्ष्यामि राज्ये त्वामृषिभिः सह .. 17 ..
text_mt: Dwell in it, O illustrious one, protecting the earth; / there I, together with the sages, will consecrate you in kingship."

sanskrit_iast:
etāvaduktvā rāmastadvākyaṃ ṛṣigaṇānvitam..
abhiṣekena divyena yojayāmāsa taṃ tadā .. 18 ..
meaning:
एतावदुक्त्वा रामस्तद्वाक्यं ऋषिगणान्वितम्..
अभिषेकेन दिव्येन योजयामास तं तदा .. 18 ..
text_mt: Having spoken this much, Rāma, with that speech accompanied by the host of sages, / endowed him then with a divine consecration.

sanskrit_iast:
uvāca ca mahātejā bhrātaraṃ dīptatejasam ..
imānyaśvasahasrāṇi catvāri bhavato'nagha .. 19..
meaning:
उवाच च महातेजा भ्रातरं दीप्ततेजसम् ..
इमान्यश्वसहस्राणि चत्वारि भवतोऽनघ .. 19..
text_mt: And he of great splendour said to his brother of radiant splendour: / "These four thousand horses are yours, O sinless one,

sanskrit_iast:
rathānāṃ dve sahasre ca dvipottamaśataṃ tathā ..
ayutaṃ ca padātīnāṃ suvarṇasya ca sañcayam .. 1.242.20 ..
meaning:
रथानां द्वे सहस्रे च द्विपोत्तमशतं तथा ..
अयुतं च पदातीनां सुवर्णस्य च सञ्चयम् .. 1.242.20 ..
text_mt: and two thousand chariots, likewise a hundred excellent elephants, / ten thousand foot-soldiers, and a store of gold,

sanskrit_iast:
antarāpaṇavīthyaśca nānāpaṇyopaśobhitāḥ ..
ādāya gaccha śatrughna paryāptabalavāhanaḥ .. 21 ..
meaning:
अन्तरापणवीथ्यश्च नानापण्योपशोभिताः ..
आदाय गच्छ शत्रुघ्न पर्याप्तबलवाहनः .. 21 ..
text_mt: and internal marketplace streets adorned with various goods— / taking [these], go, Śatrughna, with sufficient troops and vehicles!

sanskrit_iast:
balaṃ ca subhṛtaṃ vīra tuṣṭapuṣṭamanuddhatam ..
vaśaṃ ca sāntvadānābhyāṃ kuruṣva raghunandana .. 22 ..
meaning:
बलं च सुभृतं वीर तुष्टपुष्टमनुद्धतम् ..
वशं च सान्त्वदानाभ्यां कुरुष्व रघुनन्दन .. 22 ..
text_mt: Keep the army well maintained, O hero—content, nourished, and not unruly— / and bring it under control through conciliatory words and gifts, O descendant of Raghu!

sanskrit_iast:
na hyarthāstatra tiṣṭhanti na mitrāṇi na bāndhavāḥ ..
suprīto bhṛtyavargastu yatra tiṣṭhati rāghava .. 23 ..
meaning:
न ह्यर्थास्तत्र तिष्ठन्ति न मित्राणि न बान्धवाः ..
सुप्रीतो भृत्यवर्गस्तु यत्र तिष्ठति राघव .. 23 ..
text_mt: For neither wealth, nor friends, nor relatives stand by [a king] / where a well-satisfied circle of servants does not stand, O Rāghava.

sanskrit_iast:
sa tvaṃ duṣṭajanākīrṇāṃ saṃsthāpya mahatīṃ camūm ..
eka eva dhanuṣpāṇiryodhayethā madhoḥ sutam .. 24..
meaning:
स त्वं दुष्टजनाकीर्णां संस्थाप्य महतीं चमूम् ..
एक एव धनुष्पाणिर्योधयेथा मधोः सुतम् .. 24..
text_mt: Stationing that great army, crowded with corrupt folk, [outside], / fight the son of Madhu alone, bow in hand.

sanskrit_iast:
yathā ca tvāṃ na jānāti gaccha taṃ yuddhakāṅkṣiṇam ..
lavaṇaḥ sa madhoḥ putrastathā niḥśaṅkano vraja .. 25 ..
meaning:
यथा च त्वां न जानाति गच्छ तं युद्धकाङ्क्षिणम् ..
लवणः स मधोः पुत्रस्तथा निःशङ्कनो व्रज .. 25 ..
text_mt: Go to him who seeks battle in such a way that he does not know you; / proceed thus without hesitation, for he is Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu.

sanskrit_iast:
ākhyāto na ca tasyāsti kaścinmṛtyubhayānvitaḥ ..
darśanaṃ yo'bhigaccheta hanyate lavaṇena saḥ .. 26 ..
meaning:
आख्यातो न च तस्यास्ति कश्चिन्मृत्युभयान्वितः ..
दर्शनं योऽभिगच्छेत हन्यते लवणेन सः .. 26 ..
text_mt: No one filled with fear of death has ever informed him [of danger]; / whoever comes into his sight is slain by Lavaṇa.

sanskrit_iast:
māheśvareṇa śūlena viyuktaṃ mṛgayāgatam ..
dvāramāvṛtya lavaṇaṃ yudhyasva raghunandana .. 27 ..
meaning:
माहेश्वरेण शूलेन वियुक्तं मृगयागतम् ..
द्वारमावृत्य लवणं युध्यस्व रघुनन्दन .. 27 ..
text_mt: Blocking the gate when he has gone out hunting / and is separated from his trident of Maheśvara, fight Lavaṇa, O descendant of Raghu.

sanskrit_iast:
māheśvaramamoghaṃ tu śūlaṃ ca parivarjitam ..
gṛhāṇemaṃ śaraṃ vatsa sarvāyudhavināśanam .. 28 ..
meaning:
माहेश्वरममोघं तु शूलं च परिवर्जितम् ..
गृहाणेमं शरं वत्स सर्वायुधविनाशनम् .. 28 ..
text_mt: He has cast aside the unerring trident belonging to Maheśvara; / take this arrow, my child, which destroys all weapons.

sanskrit_iast:
anena lavaṇaṃ yuddhe ghātayiṣyasyasaṃśayam ..
gaccha tvaṃ grīṣmaśeṣeṇa lavaṇasya jighāṃsayā .. 29 ..
meaning:
अनेन लवणं युद्धे घातयिष्यस्यसंशयम् ..
गच्छ त्वं ग्रीष्मशेषेण लवणस्य जिघांसया .. 29 ..
text_mt: With this you will undoubtedly slay Lavaṇa in battle. / Go at the close of the hot season with the desire to slay Lavaṇa.

sanskrit_iast:
kāle tathā prāvṛṣi saṃpravṛte vivṛddhatoyāsu saridvarāsu ..
maddattabāṇena niśācarasya vyasuṃ kṣiptau pātaya tasya deham .. 1.242.30 ..

rāma uvāca ..
saṃprāpya prāvṛṣaṃ vatsa bhīmatoyadaniḥsvanām ..
niṣiddhapānthasaṃcārāṃ vidyutkṣubhitatoyadām .. 1 ..

text_mt:
Then, when the rainy season has begun in due time and the excellent rivers have their waters swollen, / with the arrow given by me cast down the lifeless body of that night-wanderer onto the ground."
1.243 / Rāma said: / "When the rainy season has arrived, my child, with the terrible roar of rain-clouds, / with the travel of wayfarers forbidden, with clouds agitated by lightning,
with the sun and moon hidden by clouds bowing under the weight of water, / with lotuses opened by the impact of torrential rain,
in which, out of terror of the excellent clouds, lovely women with full, trembling breasts / embrace their beloveds, pleasing their hearts,
the earth covered with fresh grass and adorned with cochineal insects and the like, / and the rivers overflowing and foaming with the terrible sound of their currents,
the sky, smooth and dark-blue, pervaded by water-filled rain-clouds, / white cranes adorned like stars in the autumn sky;
clouds arriving with the onset of the rains, bearing Indra's bow, / poured down upon the surface of the earth with arrow-torrents of streams of water;

on an earth where desirable and undesirable undertakings such as weddings of easy joy do not [take place], / with royal astrologers and domestic priests followed by delighted citizens,
kings become engaged in the ceremony of raising Indra's banner, / with mountains covered with fresh grass and crested with dark-blue clouds.
The earth shines with exceptional loveliness / through hills covered with fresh grass and crested with dark clouds.
Having reached that rainy season, when whole flocks of peacocks are set dancing by rumbling clouds, / take your stand at the gateway, prince, and holding your bow, slay the son of Madhu.
1.244
Rāma said:
Having slain that evil one during the rains, stay in the region of the Yamunā’s bank / and spend the autumn season there, until Janārdana awakens.
In that season the rivers are most delightful, their sandbanks laid bare, / their waters sweet and cool, adorned with Indian cranes.
Lotus ponds are adorned with lotuses resembling the morning sun; / the water of the lakes is clear, sweet, and cool.
Beds of blue water lilies, with fine petals shaped like the eyes of lovely women, / seem to gaze upon the utterly spotless sky.

text_mt:
In the vast lake of the sky, embellished with the pattern of stars, / the moon wandering at midnight shines like a wild goose.
Lifting up his great bow and drawing it tight, / autumn is seen as if filling the surface of the earth with arrows.
In the lovely rows of woodland, charming with jasmine blossoms / and bright with midday flowers, the mind attains serenity.
With ripe crops, the earth displays supreme splendor, / and sparrows rejoice along the rows of ripe fields.
Rivers, whose garments are the reed-grass, whose breasts are pairs of ruddy sheldrakes, / whose laughter is the cry of Indian cranes, kindle passion all the more.
Covered by the mass of pollen from white water lilies shaken by wild geese, / the lakes can scarcely be distinguished even by discerning men.
All the mountains, wearing cloaks of white clouds, / seem to imitate the dazzling splendor of the Snow Mountain.
Having spent autumn, rich in blue and lovely white lotuses, when the earth is adorned with fully ripened fields, / you should undertake the founding of your city when the cold season arrives.

text_mt:
Arise swiftly, go forth to victory, attain radiant fortune, O prince! / May the gods protect you at all times; place your foot upon the head of the host of foes!
1.247 / Nāḍāyana said: / Having heard these words of Rāma and saying "So be it", he in haste, / having bowed to the feet of Vasiṣṭha and of Rāma,
placing the illustrious sages headed by Bhārgava at the fore, / followed by the army as prescribed, set forth, possessing terrible prowess.
Reaching the hermitage of Vālmīki, he stayed that night there, / having honoured Vālmīki and having been honoured in turn by the sage.
On the very day Śatrughna reached the hermitage of Vālmīki, / on that very day Jānakī gave birth to twin sons.
Delighted at Sītā's delivery, that scion of Raghu in due course, / at the end of the hot season, crossed the river born of the Sun.
Having duly established his camp on the bank of the Yamunā, / bow in hand and entirely alone, he entered the forest of Madhu.

text_mt:
Having entered the dwelling of Lavaṇa there for battle, / that hero stood taking his position at the door, with his bow drawn.
At that very moment, having slain wild beasts by the thousands, / he saw the son of Madhu with a heavy load of game,
round-eyed, haughty, dreadful, biting his upper lip with his teeth, / his face formidable with fangs, of a rough appearance like an elephant.
As soon as he saw Śatrughna, he uttered many harsh words; / that evil-minded one rushed forward with the desire to slay Śatrughna.
Dropping the thousands of beasts, intent on hurling trees, / that terrifying shower of trees released by Lavaṇa,
the son of Sumitrā cut down with arrows by the hundreds and thousands. / When that great shower of trees was cut down, Lavaṇa, the tormentor of foes,
struck Śatrughna, the slayer of the foes of the gods, violently with his fist. / Then Lavaṇa, while Śatrughna was motionless from the blow of the fist,

prominent among whom are Sugrīva, Nīla, Aṅgada, the son of the Wind, Suṣeṇa, Mainda, and Dvivida, / of great strength, their bodies the size of mountains, unconquerable when engaged in battle by gods and asuras.
Śailūṣa said:
I wish to hear accurately the creation of offspring by Pulaha,
in whose lineage the monkeys, haughty with power, were born.
Nāḍāyana said:
Mṛgā, Mṛgamandā, Harī, Tāmrā, Irā,
Bhūtā, Kapiśā, Daṃṣṭrī, Surasā, and Saramā—
Kaśyapa fathered these ten daughters from Krodhā,
and they were given by Kaśyapa to the great-souled Pulaha.
I shall declare their offspring; hear them all from me.
From Mṛgā were born deer, antelopes, stags, and hares,
and ruru deer, spotted deer, antelopes, and rabbits.
From Mṛgamandā [came] sṛmaras, gayals, and buffaloes,
yaks, camels, boars, rhinoceroses, and wild asses.
From Harī were born monkeys, baboons, and kinnaras,

text_mt:
frogs, mongooses, and whatever other hole-dwelling animals there are.
Tāmrā had five daughters, and they were the wives of Varuṇa.
Pulaha, the best of the upholders of dharma and a treasury of austerities, gave them:
Śyenī, Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī.
Śyenī gave birth to a son, Sampāti,
and to Jaṭāyus, the king of vultures, haughty with strength.
Sampāti fathered hawks, vultures, and owls.
The sons of Bhāsī are known as bhāṇas; the curlews are known as sons of Krauñcī.
The offspring of Dhṛtarāṣṭrī are swans and wild geese,
as well as other water-birds with cakravāka-like faces.
The sons of Śukī are to be known as parrots and other celebrated birds.
Now, the wife of Kaśyapa who is known by the name of Irā
gave birth to an elephant, ever ready for the tasks of the gods.
The sons of Bhūtā were the bhūtas, devoted to Mahādeva:

text_mt:
the Sūcīmukhas, and the Śoṣaṇikas—these are the sixteen clans.
In these clans are born those of varied forms and movements.
In pleasure gardens, in city streets, at crossroads, and in caves,
he then gave them dwellings; [they are] endowed with disappearance and fiery energy,
[endowed with] atomicity, lightness, reach, and freedom of will.
The sons of Daṃṣṭrī are those known as fanged beasts in the world.
From Saramā came serpents and all species of insects,
as well as Śyāma and Dhavala, the two hounds, the sons of Saramā.
Those two are the attendants of Yama, possessing great strength and prowess.
Thus the progeny of Krodhā’s daughters has been declared by me.
Kaśyapa’s wife who is known by the name of Surabhi—
[among] the younger [daughters] of Śūdrā, she had two daughters:
Rohiṇī and Gandharvī, fortune attend you, O protector of the earth!
Those two were given to Pulaha by the great-souled Kaśyapa.
Surūpā, Hemarūpā, and the cow granting all desires—
upon Rohiṇī, Pulaha of great ascetic power fathered [them].

Megha, Satkumuda, Dakṣa, Sarvabhuk, and Sāmabhojana;
Gurubhāra, Kapota, Pūrvanetra, and Cirātaka,
Viṣṇugandha, Kumāra, Paribarha, and Hara;
Aśvāmbara, Madhuparka, Hemavarṇa,
Malaya, Mātariśvan, Niśākara, and Divākara.
These have been told by me only by way of example as the offspring of Garuḍa.
This is the clan of eagles, the blessed ones, O best of kings.
All these are endowed with splendor; all bear the mark of the śrīvatsa.
For this clan, O Śailūṣa, is praiseworthy, being favored by Viṣṇu.

text_mt:
Thus has been told to you the lineage of Pulaha, joined with sons and daughters;
in his lineage were born the kings of birds endowed with supreme valor, and the heroic monkeys.
1.249
Vajra said:
Through many narrations, the origin of all beings,
which destroys all sins, has been recounted to me by you.
Tell me, O Bhārgava, about their rulers among the various species,
who protect the entire threefold world, O best of the twice-born.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the creatures had thus been created, the Grandfather himself
anointed kings over each and every class [of beings].
He consecrated Soma in sovereignty
over plants, twice-born beings, constellations, sacrifices, and austerities,
just as [he consecrated] Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, over all the lords of creatures;
Dhūmra over the monkeys and bears;
the mind over all the senses; Manmatha over celestial women;
Prahlāda over all the daityas; and Yama over the ancestors.

1.250 / Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Then, on Mount Sumeru, the best of mountains, radiant with the splendor of various gems, / the Lord of Creatures, taking the aforementioned assemblies of kings,
consecrated the son of Kaśyapa in sovereignty over the gods; / and he recognized the radiant Aditya as one whose stains were dispelled.
At his consecration, Viśvakarman presented an auspicious, enchanting royal seat / shining with gems and capable of assuming any form at will.
There, having thus given instruction, Brahmā himself, the teacher of the world, / consecrated Śatakratu to the supreme lordship of the gods.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, the Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts, / the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, the hosts of Maruts,
the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, the Sādhyas, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians, / and the fortunate sages who perceive the three times with clarity,
taking what waters [they had], as did the ocean, the rivers, / the lakes with their sacred bathing sites, and the gandharvas and apsarases—

Keśava held his umbrella, which was shaped like the disc of the moon; / and the moon and the sun [held] the two white yak-tail fans.
The lord of aquatic creatures [held] the golden water vessel, the rod-bearing lord [held] the rod; / and Menakā and Rambhā [held] two charming palm-leaf fans.
And Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods, offered oblations into the fire according to the rule. / Then Pulaha himself out of affection gave him for his mount
an elephant in rut, Airāvaṇa, with four tusks; / and Pulaha gave his own son, a white steed,
and a thousand bay steeds with the speed of the wind. / Then out of affection Śrī gave an excellent chariot mount.
Agni equipped it with a golden chariot, / and next with banners of colors matching Indra's bow.
Vāyu equipped it, and Śaṅkara [equipped] the flag with an elephant. / Brahmā himself, the teacher of the world, fastened his crown.

text_mt:
And Virūpākṣa gave him shoes, O sinless one; / and an immaculate sword was given to him by Śukra, O Yādava.
And Himālaya himself, the venerable teacher of the world, gave him / the finest sandalwoods and various fragrant perfumes.
The ocean itself [gave] richly variegated jewels, / and the seasons gave him flowers and fruits.
The divine gandharvas danced and the troops of apsarases sang; / and the three worlds, with all that moves and does not move, became glad and overjoyed.
Gathering all fragrances, a fragrant wind blew. / Having gratified Bṛhaspati with a great multitude of boons,
he gratified all the best among the twice-born with hosts of boons. / For seven days he granted mental accomplishment among all living beings.
The triad of worlds was relieved of illness, death, old age, and grief; / for seven days all the torments of those dwelling in hell ceased entirely.
The entire three worlds, with all that moves and does not move, was utterly joyful. / Crowned, his limbs well-anointed, adorned with excellent earrings,

dressed in silken garments, decorated with white garlands, / Śatakratu assumed the splendor of Soma residing in the white [realm].
All the gods bowed to Śakra as he sat on the auspicious throne, / while he was being proclaimed, O great king, by the rod-bearing deity.
And the sages praised him, as did the gandharvas and apsarases. / Then Śakra, slayer of the enemies of the gods, touched auspicious objects:
a full jar, flowers, gems, clarified butter, and curds, / fruits, bilva fruit, and dug-up earth,
pleasing svastikas, nandyāvarta emblems, and gold, / and the foremost and best rivers etched in gold,
gifts turned to the north, dūrvā grass, a mirror, and clarified butter, / dharma, truth, the spear, and strength, O descendant of Yadu.
Splendour, Lakṣmī, Fortitude, Faith, Vigour, Wisdom, Action, Intellect,
embodied, attended upon the exalted Śatakratu, O scion of Yadu.

Then he bowed to his father, to his mother, to Śaṅkara, to Hari,
to Brahmā the giver of boons, the gentle one, and to the ṛṣis, O scion of Yadu.
Then, on a bright chariot driven by Mātali,
he destroyed the enemies of the gods in battle.
And in the same way he protected the entire three worlds.
This consecration of Śakra has been related to you, O scion of Yadu.

1.252
Śailūṣa said:
Explain at length the origin of the monkeys, / by whom the lineage of Pulaha appears as if adorned.
Nāḍāyana said:
The daughter of Kaśyapa named Hari, who was the wife of Pulaha, / bore from Pulaha a monkey named Śveta.
Then Śveta begot the monkey Ūrdhvadṛṣṭi; / Ūrdhvadṛṣṭi begot a tiger, and the tiger a śarabha.
The śarabha begot a bear, and the bear a monkey; / and the female bear gave birth to bears, O ruler of people,
and monkeys of huge bodies by the hundreds and thousands, / born in whose lineage were the mighty sons of the gods,
who arose to assist Rāma, who desired the slaying of Rāvaṇa. / The sister of the bear [was] the female bear; both were children of Prajāpati.

She gave birth to Dhūmra and Jāmbavant, born of bears. / Jāmbavant begot Mārjāra of terrible prowess,
and from Mārjāra were born exceedingly powerful cats in his family. / To the monkey-chief Ṛkṣa, his own mind-born daughter,
endowed with beauty and youth, the glorious Prajāpati gave. / Śakra desired her, and from that Vālin was born.
The Sun himself directly desired that very woman; / from the Sun that slender-waisted lady gave birth to Sugrīva.
Among them Vālin became the monkey king, of valiant manly strength, / who was slain by Rāma, whereas Sugrīva was consecrated.
Under his control were all the monkeys of divine origin: / Vālin's son was named Aṅgada; Hanumat was the son of the Wind;
the glorious Nīla was the son of Fire; Nala was the son of Viśvakarman; / Suṣeṇa was the son of Dharma; and Ṛṣabha was the son of Garuḍa.
Mainda and Dvivida were two heroic sons of the Aśvins; / and Dhūmra, Jāmbavant, and the monkey Vegadarśin

Śailūṣa said:
For what reason did the enmity of the monkeys with the elephants arise? / And of what nature was the battle? Relate that to me as I ask.
Nāḍāyana said:
The eight forests of elephant-lords that were told by me to you previously / were described from the ninth division of the region of Bhārata.
In all the continents, O king, and in each of the different realms, / these elephant-lords as well as the monkeys dwell in the forests.
There in the woodlands, the monkeys protect the trees; / the elephants, for mere sport, fell the trees, O lord of people.

1.254
Śailūṣa said:
All this that you have spoken repeatedly has been heard by me; / but I am not able to submit to Bharata.
One should strive upward and never bow; effort is virility itself. / Today I, devoid of all submissiveness, will not bow to anyone here.
Purposes that are achieved through excessive hardship, through transgression of dharma, / or through submission to an enemy—do not set your mind upon them!
When kingship consists of the fruit of commands, then, after bowing down, / what use is kingship to us, having the character of common people?
Having bowed to an enemy, how can a proud man, stripped of valor, / remain even within sight of his wife?
Between submitting to an enemy and dying in battle, / there is the difference that exists between killing a brahmin and the horse-sacrifice.

Having heard the words of Śailūṣa, the twice-born Nāḍāyana then / went to his own home, considering the lord of men already slain.
When Nāḍāyana had departed, the king summoned the foremost of the Gandharvas / and spoke to some, while some stood there with folded hands:
'A man who despises his enemy is destroyed very quickly.
Therefore, contempt should never be shown toward enemies. / Let some Gandharvas, haughty with strength, go to Ayodhyā.
Having gone there, quickly bring back by illusion the women / of those principal soldiers of his, of Bharata, who are of equal splendor.
Having placed the wives of those soldiers in the forefront of the battle, / I will inflict great slaughter upon them when they are dispirited.
I will cause Bharata to be killed immediately after his army is destroyed. / And let others, who are bitter enemies, go to Bharata's camp.
Let them slay his soldiers sleeping soundly at night by the thousands; / then, his army destroyed, I will kill Bharata in battle.

Likewise, let other mighty ones enter the king's palace / and slay the soldiers of Yudhājit who are sleeping soundly there.'
"I shall slay Bharata along with Yudhājit, whose army has been destroyed. / Going invisible through illusion, the Gandharvas arrogant with power
must carry out this command of mine swiftly as spoken." / Addressed thus, the Gandharvas bowed down to the lord of the earth,
took the king's order upon their heads, and set forth with swift strides. / Reaching the place designated by the ruler of the earth while day still remained,
they stirred at night, O king of kings, eager to do as commanded. / Having dispatched the Gandharvas, Śailūṣa too, in haste,
commanded his armies, "Tomorrow is battle!", O king. / And the sun went to setting, closing the lotuses; / when the world was covered with darkness, the night then began.
The king of the Gandharvas too then sported, having entered the inner quarters together with his women; / and the sons of the Gandharvas likewise sported, their pride inflamed, thinking only, "Tomorrow is battle!"

1.255 / Mārkaṇḍeya said: / The Gandharvas who were commanded to go to Ayodhyā by that king / reached Ayodhyā at midnight with swift strides.
With bodies concealed by illusion, they roamed about, O lord of the earth; / and in Ayodhyā, O great king, they beheld supreme splendour.
White as the rays of the moon, having many storeys, O descendant of Yadu, / they saw foremost mansions by the hundreds and thousands,
furnished with all manner of jewels, possessing beds and seats, / colourful with garlands of gold, and strewn with nets of pearls,
illuminated all around by blazing great lamps, / with numerous choice garlands [scented] by the emission of lamp-flames, O king.
Having entered those foremost houses, they saw human beings / with their limbs anointed with sandalwood and agallochum, adorned with all ornaments,
sporting with women like groups of gods in heaven. / And in the houses of the soldiers who had followed Bharata,
they beheld the conduct caused by longing of the women deprived of their husbands: / one, her eyes wandering, found no sleep upon her bed;

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now those Gandharvas who had been dispatched to the city named Rājagṛha / saw there an unsurpassed urban splendour.
The principal houses everywhere rivalled the moon; / they saw abundant jewels, plentiful grain and wealth.
And all around they saw the delightful city gardens / adorned with step-wells and groves of trees, O descendant of Yadu.
In the wondrous gardens the Gandharvas saw / troops of wine-drinkers following prominent men.
Along with the sounding of lutes and sweet singing, / the charming humming of six-footed bees seemed to become one [with it].
And courtesans were dancing there near the impassioned [lovers]; / elsewhere, adorned with ornaments and overcome with intoxication, they slept with their beloveds.

text_mt:
Their bodies concealed by illusory power, the Gandharvas saw there / the movements of sleeping men and women, and of men with many wives.
Some were singing, others weeping, others laughing in that very manner; / yet others, drunk with passion, were embracing one another.
Distressed and confused, some spoke indistinctly at every step; / with eyes turning aimlessly, their gaze rested nowhere on the couch.
And others had placed their arms on the shoulders of desirable women; / some engaged in quarrels, and others uttered meaningless praise.
With stumbling feet they went to a place, their minds unsteady; / some called out to crowds, while others bowed down low.
Thus in the city crowded with good people and echoing with song, / they saw the actions of men and women in the finest houses.
Urged on by female messengers, their understanding cleans[ed] in haste, / agitated, eager for wine-drinking, they went towards their beloved women.
Some drank wine together with their lovers, stirring up passion; / others made their beloveds drink, and others fed their lovers.

text_mt:
That high-minded Viṣṇu, protector of the Raghu lineage, was present in their city; / in their city there is no fear, O king, from Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, or serpents.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Returning then from Ayodhyā, from the camp, / and from Rājagṛha, all the Gandharvas reported to Śailūṣa:
“There was no talk of conflict there, nor any such protection; / it is solely through the power of Rāma and of Bharata.
Why was nothing done by us anywhere to strike, O king? / Whatever remains to be done in this matter, let the ruler of the earth do it.”
Thus addressed by the Gandharvas at the end of the night, / he quickly and promptly gave the command to prepare for action.
Then the kettle-drum of assembly was immediately struck, / at whose sound the Gandharvas approached the king’s gate.
With a large troop of elephants and an army of horses, / with chariots rumbling like clouds, and foot-soldiers fierce with fury,

text_mt:
Weapons taken up, delighting the minds of their allies with war-cries and conch-blasts, / the chiefs of the Gandharvas, of fierce fury in battle, stood waiting for Bharata.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Awakened at the end of the night, all the rulers of the earth, / longing for battle, went forth in chariots resembling cities.
with a fourfold army, sounding diverse musical instruments, / praised by bards and hailed by soldiers,
each well-accoutred individually, they arrived at the city gate. / And having performed all essential rites, the highly renowned Bharata also
went forth out of the city in a chariot of golden parts. / The driver of his chariot was his maternal uncle Yudhājit himself.
His banner shone, [bearing] a great kovidāra tree. / Having marched out with that foremost chariot, the king,
joined with all the kings and, having honored those rulers, / formed the great battle-array [called] vajra and marched forth with swift strides.

text_mt:
As that army marched, the earth seemed to tremble; / and at its immense sound the vault of the sky seemed to split.
There arose from the dust alone an unnatural, dread night. / Radiant on the earth with the brilliance of jewels on royal ornaments,
even in the darkness of the dust that army marched at its ease. / Having traversed a long road toward the sunrise,
he reached the vast, insuperable army of the gandharvas.
Those two boundless oceans of armies, like two equal dragons of dissolution, / those oceans of forces, driven by wrath, struck violent blows at each other.
1.260

Then began a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end, / causing joy to heroes and augmenting fear in the frightened.
As the army advanced there, the world was covered in dust; / nothing at all could be discerned on any side, O best of kings.
The great, tumultuous twang of sounding bows was heard, / and the blast of conches and kettledrums, and the trumpeting of elephants,

and the neighing of horses, and the roaring of heroes, / and [the clash] of weapons falling upon the armor of warriors:
“Halt, halt! You will not depart alive from the front of battle!”
“Here I stand, strike! Do you not know me?”
“Strike! Cut down! Pierce! Kill, delay not!” / Such words were heard at the front of battle.
As that dread, tumultuous battle proceeded thus, / the earthly dust that had arisen was quelled by the blood of battle.
The sky, which had earlier been covered by rising dust as if by a cloud, / then became free of dust over the field of battle, O king.
Then the heroes fought, looking upon one another, / proclaiming their lineages, heroic exploits, and names again and again.
A tumultuous clamor was heard of armies being shattered by stronger detachments of forces, / and returning once more [to the fight].
Blood was seen bespattering the variegated banners / and pennants of the kings at the front of battle.

text_mt:
As the battle thus proceeded, by gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, / by siddhas, vidyādharas, and hosts of sages on all sides,
the sky was suddenly filled, eager to witness the thunderous battle; / their immaculate aerial chariots were seen in the sky,
ringing with hundreds of tiny bells and adorned with pennants. / Then a fragrant breeze blew, carrying an auspicious scent,
and a shower of flowers fell upon the heads of the warriors there. / As it thus proceeded tumultuously, resounding with shouts and battle-cries,
foot-soldiers then slew foot-soldiers in the encounter. / Of foot-soldiers severed by the sword-edges of foot-soldiers,
limbs cut in two fell down upon the surface of the earth. / Some armored men shone forth, parrying blows of swords;
they cut the bodies of those drawing their swords, O king. / Some, their heads shattered with maces by mace-bearers upon the ground,
were seen fallen by hundreds of thousands in that battle. / Striking down enemies by hurling the remaining fragments of broken swords,

they uttered lion-roars that tore apart the enemy army. / Some, dragging each other by the hair, [striking] one another with swords,
fell dead to the earth; and others / bearing armor on their backs made armored steeds
footless in battle and slew hosts of horsemen. / Some armored men, skilled in warfare, having swiftly mounted the enemy's chariots in battle,
